source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Retrieval plus fine-tuned GPT-4 plus ensembling approaches the human crowd (3,762 questions, 5 platforms, 914 test). Raw models alone are poor forecasters.
numbers: Zero-shot/scratchpad baselines of 14 LMs: most near or worse than 0.25 Brier; best GPT-4-1106 0.208 vs crowd 0.149. Full system 0.179 Brier, accuracy 71.5% vs crowd 0.149 and 77.0%.
limits: Gap of .03 Brier to the crowd; not at crowd level overall.
agent_relevance: Without retrieval the system falls back to baseline level; the outside view needs data, not just a prompt. Base rates alone do not fix a model: feed it class records.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) prompt design, step 6
finding: The forecasting scratchpad ends with a debiasing step: check for over/under-confidence and consider the base rate. Step 4 says 'Think like a superforecaster'.
numbers: Ablation: no fine-tuning .186 vs full .179; no fine-tuning and no retrieval .206 vs best raw baseline .208. The reasoning prompt alone gave only a 'fairly minor' gain.
limits: The base-rate step was never ablated on its own.
agent_relevance: Direct precedent for an S0/S7 base-rate check in an LLM loop, but its isolated value is unmeasured. Test it alone.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) where the system beats the crowd
finding: System beats the crowd when the crowd is uncertain, retrieval is early, and many articles are found. It loses when the crowd is near-certain, because the model hedges.
numbers: Crowd in .3-.7: system .199 vs crowd .246 (validation). Near 0 or 1: system accuracy 7% higher but Brier .04 worse. All three conditions: beats crowd by >1.5 SE.
limits: Subcategory samples small. Safety-trained hedging is a hypothesis, not proven.
agent_relevance: Models under-use extreme base rates. Add a rule: when the class record is extreme, move toward it.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) ensembling and crowd blending
finding: Trimmed-mean ensembling of sampled forecasts was the best aggregator; weighting the crowd 4x with the system beat either alone.
numbers: Validation Brier: trimmed mean 0.1649, no ensemble 0.1676, USC 0.1691. Crowd+system .149 to .146 on test. RMS calibration error .42 (crowd .38).
limits: Gains are small (.003).
agent_relevance: Use trimmed-mean over N samples at S7 for probability answers; cheap structural debias.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs matched 925 human forecasters on 31 binary questions. LLMs lean toward yes.
numbers: LLM crowd mean Brier 0.20 (SD .12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD .19), t(60)=0.19, p=.850 (preregistered). Mean LLM prediction 57.35% (SD 20.93), above 50%, t(1006)=86.20, p<.001, though resolutions were nearly even.
limits: Equivalence only at medium bounds (0.081 Brier). Small question set.
agent_relevance: Acquiescence is the LLM form of ignoring how often events happen. Calibrate the yes-rate to the class base rate.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Study 2: exposure to the human median
finding: Showing the human crowd median improved GPT-4 and Claude 2, but averaging model and human was better still.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier .17 (SD .13) to .14 (SD .11), p=.003. Claude 2 .22 (SD .19) to .15 (SD .14), p<.001. Abstract: accuracy up 17% to 28%.
limits: The median acts as an anchor; models moved toward it.
agent_relevance: When a class record exists, average it with the model estimate rather than letting the model revise.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: humans vs LLMs
finding: Superforecasters beat the public and the best LLM. Top LLM runs all had the crowd forecast or a baseline value ('freeze value').
numbers: 200-question human subset: superforecasters Brier 0.096, public 0.121, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122 (p<.001). Best model without crowd forecast on market questions: 0.136. LLM set 1,000 questions.
limits: Freeze value is a current-value anchor, not a full reference class.
agent_relevance: Supplying a current reference value is what separates good from poor LLM forecasts. Put it in at S0.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench baselines
finding: Seven baselines: zero-shot, scratchpad, news, freeze values, combinations, ensembles. Freeze-value and news+freeze runs fill the top of the leaderboard.
numbers: Examples: Claude-3.5-Sonnet freeze values scratchpad .139 overall; Gemini-1.5-Pro freeze values scratchpad .123 on the larger table; 0.25 is the uninformed forecast.
limits: Different tables use different question subsets.
agent_relevance: Data-in-prompt beats thought-in-prompt for the outside view.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Prompt-induced, sequential and inherent bias in student admissions with GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-2 7B/13B. 13,465 prompts. Self-help rewriting of the prompt removed most bias in strong models.
numbers: GPT-4 admits 40.5% more students under the reject frame; Llama-2 7B labels 32.1% fewer females good at math. Self-help: GPT-4 group-attribution 0% and framing 2.7% remaining; Llama-2 7B framing 1.4%, status quo 6%; Llama-2 13B 0% and 0%.
limits: Admissions task only. Llama changed 40-52% of anchored decisions under self-help, so it was inconsistent.
agent_relevance: At S0 let a strong model rewrite the task to strip framing and anchors; weak models cannot do it reliably.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) awareness and few-shot mitigation
finding: A bias-awareness line gives small gains. Few-shot and counterfactual examples can break the model, pushing admit or reject probability to zero or one.
numbers: Awareness cut GPT-3.5 framing and status-quo biased prompts to 17.2% and 8.5%. Few-shot failures in several model and bias cells.
limits: Examples must be tailored per bias; tables are task specific.
agent_relevance: A generic 'be unbiased' line is brittle; do not use it as the only guard.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: Stronger models are consistently biased by anchor hints. Expert-labelled anchors bias them most. Simple mitigations fail.
numbers: Mean anchoring index of GPT-4 about 0.45 here vs 0.61 in a cited human-style study. No exception across 12 questions with an expert hint. Anchoring on time questions was not significant.
limits: Small custom dataset; abstract is qualitative.
agent_relevance: 'Ignore the anchor', CoT, principles and reflection all failed; gathering hints from several perspectives helped. Collect independent viewpoints before the S7 choice.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of LLMs via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Codex code generation is anchored: wrong anchor functions lower accuracy and pieces of them appear in the output.
numbers: Anchor functions lower HumanEval functional accuracy; verbatim copy of the full anchor only 4%-12% for Codex though pieces appear more often; in an estimation test the updated estimate matched the anchor exactly 67% of the time.
limits: Pre-instruction-tuned Codex; code domain.
agent_relevance: Test the agent with planted anchors before trusting its output.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld, Belinkov (2024) Instructed to Bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase decoy effect, certainty effect and belief bias in Flan-T5, Mistral, GPT-3.5, GPT-4.
numbers: Belief-bias scores for treated models range 19% to 61% compared with controls; GPT-4 reaches 84% accuracy on the belief-bias items and shows some mitigation.
limits: IT data and RLHF effects cannot be fully separated.
agent_relevance: More aligned does not mean less biased; structure around the model is still needed.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2024) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans?
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) showed anchoring, representativeness, availability, framing and endowment effects like humans.
numbers: Anchoring: low anchor mean 20.83 (ChatGPT) vs 22.5 (humans); high anchor 105.97 vs 80.50. Framing: efficacy 5 in all 11 positive trials and 4 in all 11 negative trials; humans 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<.001.
limits: Small cells (11 trials per condition); one model, early 2023.
agent_relevance: Models show the effects that structural debiasing targets, so the same fixes can be tested on them.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in LLMs
finding: Older GPT-3 models gave the intuitive wrong answer on cognitive reflection tasks. ChatGPT mostly stopped, mainly through chain of thought.
numbers: 150 CRT tasks: GPT-3-davinci correct 5%, intuitive 80%; humans 38% correct, 55% intuitive; ChatGPT-3.5 59% correct, 15% intuitive; ChatGPT-4 96% correct, 0% intuitive. CoT in 97% of GPT-3.5 and 85% of GPT-4 answers.
limits: Task set built by authors; one task family.
agent_relevance: A forced 'shortest answer' suffix cut CoT to 0%: GPT-4 correct 95% to 88%, GPT-3.5 not significant. 'Use algebra' suffix raised GPT-3 correct 5% to 28%. A built-in reasoning step beats warning the model.

source: Li et al. (2023) EmotionPrompt (incentive-like stimuli)
finding: Adding lines such as 'This is very important to my career' improved outputs on 45 tasks across 6 models.
numbers: 8.00% relative gain on Instruction Induction, 115% on BIG-Bench; human study, 106 participants: 10.9% average gain on performance, truthfulness, responsibility. Relative gain by model (Table 6): Vicuna 9.58, Llama 2 6.00, ChatGPT 4.32, GPT-4 0.85, Bloom 0.51, Flan-T5-Large 0.28.
limits: Strong models have high baselines so gains shrink; text prompts only.
agent_relevance: Machine form of 'incentives raise effort'. Works on weaker models, little on GPT-4. Test before adding.

source: Li et al. (2023) EmotionPrompt best stimulus differs by task
finding: On Instruction Induction EP02 ('This is very important to my career') is best; on BIG-Bench EP06 is best.
numbers: Best stimulus beats the worst by 6.06% on Instruction Induction.
limits: Best line differs by benchmark.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code one motivation line.

source: Salinas & Morstatter (2024) The Butterfly Effect of Altering Prompts (tipping)
finding: Offering a tip improved Llama-7B; ChatGPT showed minimal difference. A $1000 tip lowered accuracy compared with smaller tips.
numbers: Tipping $1, $10, or $100 significantly improved Llama-7B over every other variation tested; minimal change for ChatGPT.
limits: Classification tasks; table columns garbled in text extraction so per-cell values are not recorded.
agent_relevance: Incentive text is an unreliable lever; large models are more robust to spurious tokens. Treat as noise to test.

source: Bsharat, Myrzakhan, Shen (2023) Principled Instructions Are All You Need
finding: 26 prompt principles, including 'I'm going to tip $xxx for a better solution!' and 'You will be penalized'.
numbers: On the ATLAS benchmark principles raised GPT-4 quality by 57.7% and correctness by 36.4% on average; gain grows with model size (over 20% from LLaMA-2-7B to GPT-4).
limits: Bundle result; tip line not isolated; hand-built benchmark.
agent_relevance: The incentive-line effect cannot be separated from this paper.

source: Zou et al. (2022) Autocast, as cited in Halawi et al. (2024)
finding: Earlier automated forecasting system on Autocast (Metaculus, INFER, GJOpen).
numbers: Accuracy 65.4% vs community 92.8%; improved to 67.9% by Yan et al. (2024); Halawi system 71.5% on harder questions (crowd 77.0%).
limits: Known only through the Halawi citation.
agent_relevance: Shows progress of outside-view forecasting systems from 2022 to 2024.

source: Tetlock & Gardner (2015) Superforecasting, as cited for the base-rate prompt step
finding: Halawi et al. cite this book for the 'consider historical base rates' step. Superforecasters start from the class base rate, then adjust.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; only the citation inside Halawi was read.
agent_relevance: Reference for the S0 gate.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 on vignette-based decision tasks.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Unopened; flagged for later.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a later pass.

source: Gap note: accountability (Lerner and Tetlock) not found tested on LLMs
finding: No paper found that tests accountability or audit-threat prompts on LLMs as a named manipulation. Nearest: awareness prompts (Echterhoff), base-rate step (Halawi), freeze values (Karger).
numbers: Search tools were rate-limited (arXiv API 429, OpenAlex budget gone, WebSearch budget gone); search was by known paper only.
limits: Absence is not proven.
agent_relevance: Open ground: test 'a reviewer will check this' lines against none on a judgment set.

source: Gap note: no LLM agent retrieves a reference class and computes its outcome rate
finding: Nearest implementations are the Karger freeze value and the Halawi base-rate reminder. None retrieves N similar past cases and takes their outcome distribution.
numbers: None.
limits: Search limits as above.
agent_relevance: Candidate new operator for S7: retrieve class record, then adjust from it.

source: Synthesis: what changes LLM bias (Echterhoff, Lou, Hagendorff, Halawi)
finding: Adding information or a reasoning step beats telling the model not to be biased.
numbers: Ignore-anchor failed (Lou); few-shot broke decisions (Echterhoff); CoT raised GPT-3 correct 5% to 28% (Hagendorff); retrieval moved Brier .206 to .179 (Halawi).
limits: Different tasks and models; the synthesis is ours.
agent_relevance: Prefer scaffolds that change the input or add a step.

source: Synthesis: incentives on LLMs (Li; Salinas; Bsharat)
finding: Incentive-type lines help small models, little for strong ones, and can hurt at extreme levels.
numbers: EmotionPrompt gain 9.58 Vicuna vs 0.85 GPT-4; tip helped Llama-7B but not ChatGPT; $1000 tip lowered accuracy.
limits: Mixed benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Cheap but noisy; measure per model.
